newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - ConEd earnings more volatile-CFO.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - ConEd earnings more volatile-CFO.

text.p: Increased earnings volatility will be one result of Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc's restructuring settlement with New York regulators, Chief Financial Officer Joan S. Freilich told Reuters.

She told the company's annual meeting Monday, the utility achieved its three major financial goals in negotiations with the New York Public Service Commission staff -- a balance between keeping rates as low as possible while protecting the company's financial strength, recovery of investments and commitments made in the past, and an opportunity to grow.
In return the utility gave up the operating incentives and weather normalization clause of its previous rate agreement, Freilich said in an interview.
"We expect everything is retroactive to April 1," she added, noting this means the resulting volatility and reduced return on equity will be effective with results for the current quarter.

Under an agreement with the commission, she explained, Con Edison began accounting for second quarter results as though the settlement agreement were in effect. The commission has said it expects to have a decision in June.
The weather normalization clause was designed to level out the impact of warmer or colder than normal temperatures on Con Edison's revenues.
A limited look at the impact of weather came in the first quarter when warmer than normal temperatures, compared to colder than normal in 1996, cut steam revenues 14.5 percent.

Although steam accounts for less than 6 percent of annual revenues, this swing was enough to reduce earnings by $0.03 per share in the first quarter -- a third of the decline of $0.09 from 1996's initial three months to $0.69 per share.
The remaining $0.06, Freilich said when the earnings were reported, was the lower return on equity in the second year of Con Edison's 1995 rate agreement.

She said the settlement rate structure is based on a return on equity much closer to the 10.6 percent called for in the utility's latest steam case than the 12.3 percent earned in 1996 or the 11.9 percent earned in the 12 months ended March 31.

She also pointed out the "agreement shifts significant (financial) on to the company," including five years without a rate change -- "the longest we've ever been" away from seeking commission approvals of rate changes.
"Overall," Freilich told the annual meeting, the agreement should provide us with the opportunity to earn a fair return for our shareholders."

She noted that constructuction spending, which had dropped to $675 million in 1996 from the $800 million level five years ago, "will be down to $600 million (for the regulated transmission and distribution operations) by the year 2000."
Such spending is budgeted at $660 million this year and $620 million in 1998, the company's annual report said.

Included in the outlays this year and in the next four years is $1.5 billion in new transmission and distribution investment over five years, including $375 million a year in 1997 and 1998, spokesman Richard Mulieri said.
